newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-TOURNOI PROVIDED PERFECT APPETISER FOR FRANCE'98.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-TOURNOI PROVIDED PERFECT APPETISER FOR FRANCE'98.

text.p: If the main course of the World Cup is as appetizing next summer as the hors d'oeuvre of the Tournoi de France, soccer fans are in for a real treat.

A vastly improved England, flashes of brilliance from world champions Brazil, question marks over hosts France and an indifferent display from an under-prepared Italy all served to whet the appetite for the biggest World Cup in history.

Of course, matches next June and July will be more serious with tactics more restrained than in the Tournoi. But even so, 16 goals in six games, a good atmosphere in the stadiums, and growing excitement in the World Cup venues all augur well for France '98.
Like the US'93 Cup a year before the last World Cup and the Umbro Cup a year before Euro '96, the Tournoi was as much a dress rehearsal for the organisers of the main event as for the players.
England were the surprise of the week, securing the crystal trophy with a match to spare for their first high profile international success since they won the World Cup in 1966.

But no-one in the England camp is reading too much into it. They know they still have to go to Italy and win a difficult qualifier in Rome in October to ensure automatic qualification for the World Cup.
Failing that, they could qualify automatically as the best placed of the runners-up in the European group competition. At the very least, they will have a place in the runner-up play-offs.

But England coach Glenn Hoddle was a delighted man on Wednesday. Speaking at a British Embassy reception in Paris he said: "I never doubted for a second the value of coming here, and I am very very pleased England were invited.
"People who said we would gain nothing from it were wrong. There are only 12 months to go to the World Cup, and we have learned some very valuable lessons indeed and made a lot of progress."
Sir Bobby Charlton, England's record goalscorer with 49 goals in 106 appearances between 1958 and 1970 added: "In some ways, it wasn't such a bad thing for England to lose to Brazil on Tuesday.
"After beating Italy and France, if England had won all three matches the pressure to come back and win the World Cup next year would have been almost too much.
"This way we still have something to prove, something to achieve."
Michel Platini, co-president of the French organising committee said he had been very impressed with the England team, "but I would be a hypocrite if I said I wanted them to do as well next year.
"Brazil were also very interesting. Sometimes they are a little frustrating, sometimes they are excellent. But they are always the team to beat."

Brazil's 3-3 draw with Italy in Lyon on Sunday was the outstanding match, a thriller many wished had been the 1994 World Cup final rather than the sterile 0-0 draw before Brazil won the World Cup on penalties.

Sepp Blatter, speaking as a fan rather than Fifa's secretary general, said: "That was a truly memorable game, a wonderful advert for football and showed just what players can achieve with no real tactical restraints put on them in a tournament such as this.
"Next year it will be far more serious of course, but that was a match to savour."
Brazil finished second with a win and two draws. France and Italy both drew twice and lost once to finish third and bottom respectively.

French manager Aime Jacquet, under increasing pressure to forge a side capable of winning the World Cup, admitted he had plenty of work to do. Italian coach Cesare Maldini said repeatedly his team's performance here would have little impact on their planning for 1998 as they were tired after a long season and under-prepared.

Although Brazil as defending champions, and France as hosts, are automatically qualified for the World Cup, Italy still have to see off England in their qualifier to take their spot. England's 2-0 win over Italy last Wednesday hinted the Italians might not have things all their own way in Rome.
Off the field, both FIFA and the organising committee hinted that some compromise may be reached with the legal authorities over the removal of perimeter fences before the World Cup.

Also, the organisers at Lyon learned lessons about security, traffic and crowd management following confusion at the first game between France and Brazil. Conditions were improved for the second match at Lyon between Brazil and Italy five days later.
